nameStory: The Common Bellowsfish gets its name from its ability to inflate parts of its body like the bellows of an old blacksmith's forge. The alternate name 'snipefish' comes from its incredibly long, pointed snout that resembles the bill of a snipe bird, perfect for probing into crevices for tiny prey.
description: The Common Bellowsfish is a peculiar-looking fish with an unmistakable long, needle-like snout and a distinctively tall, blade-like dorsal spine that juts up from its back. Its body is laterally compressed (flattened from side to side) and has an almost triangular profile when viewed from the side. This unusual fish is quite small, typically measuring just a few inches in length, making it easy to overlook despite its distinctive features.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely compressed, almost paper-thin body that feels rigid to the touch, with a distinctive triangular profile and sharp edges along the belly

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Extraordinarily long, tubular snout that extends far beyond the body length, feeling hard and inflexible like a thin stick

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Prominent, knife-like first dorsal spine that projects upward and backward, sharp enough to prick your finger if handled carelessly

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Silvery to pinkish body with a metallic sheen that catches light, often appearing translucent with visible internal structures

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Quite small, rarely exceeding 4-6 inches total length including the extended snout, fitting easily in your palm

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deeper offshore waters, often swimming in small schools near the bottom or mid-water column

habitat: In New England waters, Common Bellowsfish are typically found in deeper offshore areas beyond the continental shelf, usually at depths of several hundred feet. They prefer cooler waters and are occasionally brought up by deep-sea fishing operations or found washed ashore after storms. These fish are more commonly encountered in the warmer waters south of Cape Cod.

seasonality.spring: May be found in slightly shallower waters as they follow prey movements, occasionally caught by deep-sea fishing vessels operating off the coast.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter specimens in New England waters, when warmer currents may bring them closer to our region from southern waters.
seasonality.fall: Specimens may occasionally wash ashore during storm events, particularly after nor'easters that churn up deep-water areas.
seasonality.winter: Rarely encountered in New England waters during the coldest months, as they likely move to deeper or more southern waters.

funFact: Despite being called a 'bellowsfish,' these fish don't actually inflate like pufferfish – the name comes from their ability to rapidly extend their snout like a telescope, creating a bellows-like pumping action to suck up tiny crustaceans and plankton!
confusionNotes: The Common Bellowsfish is so distinctive with its incredibly long snout and prominent dorsal spine that it's unlikely to be confused with any other New England fish. The closest might be a pipefish, but pipefishes have much more elongated, snake-like bodies and lack the prominent dorsal spine.
contextualKnowledge: The Common Bellowsfish is also known by several other names including longspine snipefish, spine trumpet fish, and even trumpetfish, which can be confusing since true trumpetfish are much larger Caribbean species. This naming confusion reflects the fish's unusual appearance that has inspired many different descriptive common names.
compareHints: The Common Bellowsfish is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making it unique in the region. Compared to other members of the snipefish family found elsewhere, it's distinguished by its particularly prominent dorsal spine and more compressed body shape. Other snipefishes may have longer snouts relative to body size or different spine arrangements.
